title: Vail Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Vail well records show a 55-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock and permit history still matter when buying or building.
h1: What Vail Well Records Say About Depth, Water and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Vail means looking past the listing’s phrase “private well.” Records within 5 miles show 244 permitted wells, but only 75 are recorded as constructed, 95 report a total depth, 17 report a pump yield, and 9 report a static water level. That limited reporting matters. The local numbers point to generally shallow wells and strong reported yields, while the fractured mountain bedrock makes any individual lot less predictable.

Use these figures to check a seller’s well file, compare nearby permits, and set realistic expectations for a new-well bid. Minturn, Avon, and Red Cliff are the closest named areas in the records, with Edwards, Copper Mountain, and Silverthorne providing additional regional context.

sections.heading: Vail well depth is usually shallow, but bedrock controls the outcome
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Vail is 55 feet. The middle half runs from 36 to 85 feet, and 78% of wells are under 100 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. The record also includes wells reaching 200 feet at the 90th percentile and a deepest recorded well of 475 feet.

Most permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 227 wells in that category. In granite and gneiss, water-bearing fractures can be unevenly distributed. A neighboring shallow well may not predict the depth on your lot. Ask for completion reports near the parcel and have a driller price the possibility of going substantially deeper.

sections.heading: Reported Vail well yields are strong, with a small data set
sections.html:
Only 17 wells report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are not a guarantee for all Vail properties. Among those records, the median is 200.0 gallons per minute and the middle half spans 20.0 to 750.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-eight percent report 15 or more gallons per minute, while 12% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. None of the reported wells are under 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures suggest that a tested well can produce substantially more than ordinary household demand, but production varies sharply in fractured rock. Confirm the actual well test, pump size, storage, and permitted use. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to Colorado’s 35-gpm pumping limit, even if the formation can produce more.

sections.heading: Vail water levels look shallow, but there is no reliable trend
sections.html:
Nine permitted wells report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 16 feet, with the middle half from 12 to 20 feet. That is encouraging for pump installation and excavation on those recorded wells, but it should not be treated as a groundwater map for every Vail lot.

The permit history does not provide enough static-water observations by decade to establish a rising or dropping water table. A buyer should request the original well construction and test documents, then compare them with nearby permits in Vail, Minturn, Avon, and Red Cliff. Water levels can also differ across short distances in fractured mountain terrain.

sections.heading: Permit history shows sustained drilling around Vail
sections.html:
Permit records begin in the 1960s, with 3 permits in that decade and 10 in the 1970s. The count rose to 25 in the 1980s and 67 in the 1990s, followed by 27 in the 2000s, 35 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s. The newest permit in this data set is from 2023.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 73 wells; Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. (Lensch, George E), with 12; and Buena Vista Drilling (Shelton, William L), with 7. These are record names, not a recommendation. Before relying on a seller’s claim, obtain the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, pump test, and current operating information.

sections.heading: A Vail well at the median depth may cost $9,600 to $17,500 finished
sections.html:
Vail’s fractured granite and gneiss make drilling slower and less predictable than work in softer ground. The cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,600 to $5,500.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $9,600 to $17,500 at that depth. A bid can rise quickly if the hole must reach 200 feet or more, if access is difficult, or if the site needs additional rock excavation. Ask what the price includes: casing, grout, pump equipment, testing, power, trenching, and work needed to connect the house.

sections.heading: Environmental, septic, and dry-hole checks belong in the purchase review
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 47 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a problem at a specific property, but they justify a water-quality test and a review of nearby land uses, mine workings, and site drainage.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured bedrock even though the reported wells show strong yields. Confirm well location, casing, grout, pump performance, and recent laboratory results. A septic system also needs adequate separation from the well and suitable soil and slope. Before building, verify the well’s permitted use, power access, driveway route, trenching conditions, and the county’s septic and site-development requirements.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Vail, Colorado?
faq.a: Recorded wells within 5 miles of Vail have a median depth of 55 feet, with the middle half from 36 to 85 feet. Most, 78%, are under 100 feet. The record also includes wells at 200 feet or deeper, including the deepest recorded well at 475 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the depth on one lot difficult to predict from the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Vail?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At Vail’s 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,600 to $5,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $9,600 to $17,500. Difficult mountain access or a deeper hole can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Vail wells produce?
faq.a: Only 17 permitted wells report a pump yield, so the figures are a limited sample. The reported median yield is 200.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 20.0 to 750.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-eight percent report 15 or more gallons per minute, and none report under 5 gallons per minute. Verify the specific well test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Vail?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Vail well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped sites include 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 47 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, review nearby land uses, and retest if conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well in Vail?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a well permit. Confirm the well’s permitted use and production, then evaluate septic soils, separation from the well, driveway access, trenching, electrical service, and mountain excavation. The Vail records show 9% domestic or household use and 54% monitoring use, so a nearby permit may not support a home without further review.
